core.big_idea: The Davidic promise created hope for a lasting ruler within God's story.

passages.reading_note: Read the promise in its immediate setting, including David, his offspring, discipline, house, kingdom, and throne.
Use selected verses to see the promise celebrated before the psalm later laments apparent failure.
Use to show the New Testament applying Davidic throne language to Jesus.

core.metanarrative_position: Davidic covenant: God's promise establishes royal hope that survives the failures of individual kings and is applied to Jesus in the New Testament.
core.biblical_genre: Royal narrative, covenant promise, and poetry

claims.statement: God reminded David that He had taken him from shepherding and had been with him.
God promised to raise up David's offspring, establish his kingdom, and establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
The promise includes father-son language and discipline for wrongdoing, showing an immediate royal line as well as enduring hope.
The New Testament applies Davidic throne language to Jesus.
Christian interpretation sees Jesus as the ultimate fulfilment of the enduring throne promise, while Jewish and other readings do not accept that identification.
claims.credible_alternative: Jewish interpretation can understand the promise in relation to David's dynasty and future messianic hope without identifying Jesus as the Messiah.
claims.interpretive_hinge: How later canonical texts identify Jesus in relation to David and how forever language functions across dynasty, exile, and messianic expectation.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not pretend 2 Samuel 7 names Jesus directly or erase the immediate reference to David's royal offspring.

core.interpretation_skill: Read promise in immediate context, trace later canonical use, and distinguish direct wording from Christian messianic synthesis.

learning.foundation_objective: Explain the main parts of God's promise to David and place the Davidic covenant on the whole-Bible timeline.
learning.extension_objective: Distinguish the immediate royal-line meaning from the New Testaments identification of Jesus as the enduring Davidic ruler.
know: David wanted to build a house for God.
God promised to build David's house or dynasty.
The promise included offspring, kingdom, and throne.
understand: Biblical promises can have an immediate historical horizon and a wider canonical fulfilment.
Human kings fail, but the royal hope remains in God's story.
practise: Read later passages before claiming fulfilment.
Place hope in God's promise rather than idealising a human leader.
become: A student who traces promise carefully and resists turning political leaders into messianic figures.
success_evidence: The student lists offspring, house, kingdom, and throne.
The student places David before exile and Jesus.
The student labels direct text and canonical synthesis.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students explain the Davidic promise and how the New Testament connects it to Jesus.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: How can the word house mean both a building and a family line?
say: David wanted to build a house for God, but God promised to build David's house or dynasty.
The promise includes offspring, kingdom, throne, father-son relationship, and discipline.
Later kings failed and the monarchy collapsed, but the promise continued to shape hope.
Luke applies Davidic throne language to Jesus, and Christians understand Him as the enduring King.
ask: Which parts of the promise concern David's offspring?
Which later text connects the promise to Jesus?
zero_prep_card.do: Use the Promise Layers chart: David, Royal Line, Crisis, Jesus.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for careful reading, hope in God's faithfulness, and allegiance to Jesus rather than political saviours.

preparation.passage_context: Second Samuel 7 follows David's establishment in Jerusalem and his desire to build a temple. Through Nathan, God reverses David's proposal: David will not secure God with a house; God will establish David's house. The passage speaks both to an immediate son and to an enduring dynasty.
text_observations: God's past action and presence precede the future promise.
House shifts from temple to dynasty.
Offspring, father-son language, wrongdoing, discipline, steadfast love, kingdom, and throne appear together.
The word forever creates the later interpretive tension when the monarchy collapses.
interpretation_notes: Do not skip the immediate royal line by moving directly to Jesus.
Use Luke 1 as a later canonical interpretation rather than pretending 2 Samuel uses New Testament terminology.
Psalm 89 can be used to show how faithful readers wrestled with promise and apparent historical collapse.
theological_guardrails: Do not identify a modern nation, dynasty, or political leader as the automatic continuation of David's throne.
Do not describe every detail of Solomon's reign as a complete messianic fulfilment.
Do not dismiss Jewish readings with caricature; state the Christian canonical case accurately.

likely_questions.question: Did the promise fail when Judah lost its king?
likely_questions.purpose: Explain that exile created the central tension. Biblical prophets, psalms, and the New Testament continue to interpret the promise as unresolved hope rather than simple cancellation.

likely_questions.question: Does forever mean every king would rule forever?
likely_questions.purpose: No individual Davidic king lived forever. The term concerns the enduring house, kingdom, and throne promise, whose full interpretation develops canonically.

discussion_questions.question: How does the meaning of house change in the passage?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: From a building to a family dynasty.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain the rhetorical reversal between David's plan and God's promise.

discussion_questions.question: Which details point to an immediate royal son?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why immediate fulfilment cannot simply be erased.

discussion_questions.question: What creates hope beyond one failed king?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: The enduring house, kingdom, and throne.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Trace how exile turns forever language into a major biblical question.

discussion_questions.question: How does Luke 1 use the promise?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: It applies David's throne and endless kingdom to Jesus.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Distinguish quotation, allusion, and theological identification.

activities.title: Davidic Promise Layers
steps: Record the immediate promise to David's offspring.
Add the royal line and its failures.
Add exile as the historical crisis.
Add Luke 1 and the Christian claim about Jesus.
activities.learning_link: Prevents collapse of immediate and canonical horizons.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Create four headings on a board.

activities.title: Claim Classification Drill
steps: Classify a direct phrase from 2 Samuel 7.
Classify a historical statement about exile.
Classify Luke 1s use as canonical synthesis.
Classify the Christian conclusion about Jesus as framework position supported by the New Testament.
activities.learning_link: Practises text, history, synthesis, and framework distinctions.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Call out claims and use hand signals for categories.

closing.prayer_prompt: Thank God for faithfulness and ask for hope centred on Jesus rather than human power.
closing.take_home_line: God's promise to David created hope for an enduring King.

family.title: A House That Means a Dynasty
family.parent_intro: This study traces the promise from David to later Christian identification of Jesus without skipping the immediate context.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Circle house, offspring, kingdom, throne, and forever. Ask what each means in context.
Make four cards: David, Royal Line, Exile, Jesus, and explain the connection.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What is directly promised in 2 Samuel?
What does Luke add to the Christian interpretation?

interactive.title: Promise Layers
interactive.instructions: Arrange four cards and label direct text, historical development, and canonical synthesis.

family.weekly_action: When discussing a leader this week, avoid saviour language and remember that allegiance to Jesus is primary.
family.prayer: God, thank You for keeping Your purposes through human failure. Teach us to hope in Jesus the King.
family.parent_note: Avoid mapping the promise directly onto modern politics or treating one party, nation, or leader as the kingdom of God.

quiz.question: In 2 Samuel 7, what second meaning does house take?
quiz.explanation: God promises to establish David's house.

quiz.question: The promise includes discipline for wrongdoing.
quiz.explanation: Father-son language includes correction, showing an immediate royal line.

quiz.question: Which New Testament passage applies Davidic throne language to Jesus?
quiz.explanation: Luke explicitly names David's throne and an endless kingdom.

quiz.question: Which statement is the Christian canonical synthesis?
options: Jesus is the enduring Davidic King
David wanted to build a house

answer.text: Jesus is the enduring Davidic King

quiz.explanation: That conclusion depends on later canonical identification.

puzzle.title: Promise Through the Story
puzzle.instructions: Place the stages in canonical order.
items: Jesus is announced as Davidic King.
God promises David's house and throne.
The monarchy fails and exile creates a crisis.
David's royal line continues through history.
God promises David's house and throne.
David's royal line continues through history.
The monarchy fails and exile creates a crisis.
Jesus is announced as Davidic King.

printables.title: Davidic Promise Layers
printables.purpose: Separate immediate royal meaning, historical development, and Christian canonical fulfilment.

accessibility.reading_level: Upper-primary discussion with concrete anchors before abstract explanation.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Define covenant, genre, inference, and other technical terms before expecting use.
neurodiversity_supports: Use a visible timeline or comparison grid.
Allow written, drawn, or spoken responses.
Model one completed example before independent work.
sensory_notes: Offer a seated alternative to movement activities.
non_reader_support: Use prepared cards so participation does not depend on fluent reading.

do_not_ask: Do not ask students to identify a current leader as God's chosen king.
Do not mock Jewish or other non-Christian readings.
Do not equate loyalty to Jesus with party allegiance.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Keep contemporary examples general and return to text, canonical use, and evidence classification.
